svg.aria-label: Vertical temperature scale in Fahrenheit and Celsius showing what mosquitoes do at each temperature, from heat stress above 100 degrees Fahrenheit down to a hard freeze at 28 degrees Fahrenheit
svg.title: What mosquitoes do at each temperature, in Fahrenheit and Celsius
svg.desc: Mosquitoes are cold-blooded. Above 100 degrees Fahrenheit (38 Celsius) they stop flying in open sun and shelter in shade. Above 95 Fahrenheit (35 Celsius) adults enter heat stress and lifespan shortens. From 80 to 95 Fahrenheit (27 to 35 Celsius) biting and breeding peak. From 70 to 80 Fahrenheit (21 to 27 Celsius) is the preferred range, which is also the temperature of an air-conditioned house. Below 60 Fahrenheit (15 Celsius) they fly poorly. At 50 Fahrenheit (10 Celsius) they stop flying and feeding. Around 46 to 53 Fahrenheit (8 to 12 Celsius) larvae stop developing and begin dying. At 32 Fahrenheit (0 Celsius) a light frost stuns adults. At 28 Fahrenheit (minus 2 Celsius) a hard freeze kills active adults, but eggs and hibernating females survive.
svg.text: What mosquitoes do at each temperature
°F first, °C in brackets. Mosquitoes are cold-blooded, so activity tracks air temperature almost directly.

g.text: Too hot to fly in the open — they hide in shade, mulch and crawl spaces
Heat stress begins — lifespan shortens, egg output falls, dehydration risk
Peak biting and fastest larval growth — the worst band for a homeowner
The preferred range — also the temperature of an air-conditioned house
Slowing — clumsy flight, biting pressure drops noticeably
The switch — below this they stop flying, host-seeking and feeding
Larvae stop developing and start dying — long before the water freezes
Light frost stuns exposed adults — many recover when it warms back up
Hard freeze kills active adults — eggs and hibernating females survive it

svg.text: A hard freeze ends the flying season. It does not end the population — eggs and diapausing females restart it in spring.
Thresholds vary a few degrees by species. Sources: CDC, EPA, AMCA, NOAA/National Weather Service. Diagram: BuzzSkito.
